Speculation About the Past

You can use modals to talk about degrees of certainty and speculate about things in the past.
You use them to describe what is definite, probable, possible, or impossible from the speaker's point of view.
You can use must, may, might, and could to describe degrees of certainty.
You can use modals with the Present Perfect to talk about the possibility of a past event that is not clear in the present context.
Example:
The examiner must have known she was nervous, because her hands were shaking.

• May have has a slightly stronger meaning that might have or could have.
  • You can add not to make a negative speculation (It may not have been true).
The examiner must have known she was nervous, because her hands were shaking.
When he spoke, she realized that she may have met him somewhere before.
Elaine knew that he couldn't have been the tester during her previous tests, but who was he?
Where could she have heard it before?
She might have heard him in the testing office the last time, she decided.
Talking About the Past: The Simple Past, The Present Perfect and the Past Continuous Tenses
When you tell stories and anecdotes, it is common to use a mixture of tenses. This allows you to convey a variety of timelines and action sequences.
You use the Simple Past tense to talk about many kinds of past events: short, quickly finished actions, longer situations and repeated events.

For example:
During the first test, she forgot to turn on a directional signal.
She started up the car.

You use the Present Perfect tense to talk about a past action or an action that began in the past that is connected to the present in some way. It is common to use for and since when referring to time periods in the Present Perfect.

For example:
Elaine has taken her driving exam twice. Since then, Elaine has taken ten additional driving lessons.
You use the Past Continuous tense to talk about an action that was happening at a time before now and to describe the background in a story written in the past tense.

For example:
During the second test, she was parking when she realized the space was too small.
She was concentrating on driving.

images.text:
Elaine has taken her driving exam twice. During the first test, she forgot to turn on a directional signal. During the second test, she was parking when she realized the space was too small. Since then, Elaine has taken ten additional driving lessons. She has been practicing for weeks. If she hadn't already failed two driving tests, she wouldn't feel so nervous now.

So, here Elaine was, taking her test again. It was torture! The examiner must have known she was nervous, because her hands were shaking. He was sitting calmly, in a blue cardigan, smiling at her. When he spoke, she realized that she may have met him somewhere before.

Elaine knew that he couldn't have been the tester during her previous tests, but who was he? She couldn't place his voice. Where could she have heard it before? She might have heard in him in the testing office the last time, she decided.

Elaine didn't have any more time to pay attention to the tester. She started up the car and then she was concentrating on driving. To her astonishment, she handled the car well and even parked without any problem.

When she stepped out of the car, the tester smiled again and said, “You've passed the test!” She was stunned!

When she got home, she turned on the TV. An advertisement for safe driving she had seen countless times was on. She recognized the voice. The "safe driver" sitting behind the wheel in the advertisement was her tester.
